idiom_name: reply channel carried in the request (resultChan)
implementation_notes: Go has no token type to build: the ACT is a first-class value - the request's own reply channel. The form shown in Effective Go is a request struct with a resultChan chan T field; the client reads from it, the goroutine that performs the operation writes the result exactly once, and the receiver demultiplexes in constant time with no registry and no lookup by request id (the same document calls it 'safe, parallel demultiplexing'). Buffered channels are what make the token robust: make(chan T, 1) lets the producer finish even if the receiver has already given up. Cancellation and propagation travel separately in context.Context (its receive-only Done channel), fan-in aggregation in sync.WaitGroup, and arbitration between several possible completions in select.
pitfalls: Goroutines are not garbage collected: if the receiver abandons the wait, an unbuffered reply channel blocks its producer forever - size the channel (make(chan T, 1)) or give the sender a cancellation path.
A channel token is single-shot; closing it broadcasts (right for cancellation, wrong for a per-request completion) and sending on a closed channel panics.
Tokens created inside a loop were capture-unsafe before Go 1.22, where the loop variable is shared across all goroutines - a completion could be attributed to the wrong request.
A derived context lives until its parent is cancelled unless the returned CancelFunc is called (the -lostcancel vet check), so a leaked cancel keeps the token's request state reachable.
